zebralogic.title: Consolidate Direct Equivalences
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly equates two attribute values (e.g., "the Xiaomi Mi 11 user is short"), treat them as belonging to the same entity and assign both attributes together.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue states that one attribute value equals another attribute value.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the phone "Xiaomi Mi 11" to house 3 and the height "short" to house 5, ignoring that the clue makes them the same person.

zebralogic.title: Assign Fixed Positions Immediately
zebralogic.principle: If a clue fixes an attribute to a specific house number, place that attribute at that house right away and propagate any linked attributes.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "X is in house N" or "the Y is directly left of house N".
zebralogic.example: Delaying the placement of "Samsung Galaxy S21 is in house 2" until later, which later creates a conflict with the adjacency chain.

zebralogic.title: Translate 'N houses between' to Exact Distance
zebralogic.principle: Convert statements like "there are N houses between X and Y" into the exact distance constraint |pos(X) − pos(Y)| = N + 1.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue mentions a specific number of houses separating two entities.
zebralogic.example: Treating "two houses between A and B" as merely "A is left of B" and allowing them to be adjacent, violating the exact distance.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Adjacency for 'next to' and Ordered Left
zebralogic.principle: Translate "next to", "directly left of", and similar phrasing into precise adjacency constraints (|pos(A) − pos(B)| = 1) or ordered constraints (pos(A) = pos(B) − 1).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses adjacency or ordering language.
zebralogic.example: Reading "Alice is directly left of the person whose child is Fred" as a loose left‑of relation and placing them non‑adjacent.

zebralogic.title: Treat Consecutive Chains as a Block
zebralogic.principle: When several adjacency clues form a sequence (e.g., A left of B left of C), treat the whole sequence as a fixed block whose internal order is known, reducing the search space.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When multiple adjacency or ordering clues involve the same set of entities.
zebralogic.example: Handling "Google Pixel 6 left of iPhone 13" and "iPhone 13 left of Samsung" as independent constraints, missing that the three phones occupy three consecutive houses.

zebralogic.title: Propagate Linked Attribute Pairs
zebralogic.principle: Whenever a clue links two attributes of the same entity (e.g., "Carol uses OnePlus 9"), immediately assign both attributes to that entity and propagate any further implications.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue states that a specific person or object has a particular attribute.
zebralogic.example: Assigning Carol's name to a house but forgetting to also set her phone to OnePlus 9, later causing a conflict.

zebralogic.title: Output Solution in Expected JSON Table Format
zebralogic.principle: Produce a JSON object with top‑level keys "header" (list of column names) and "rows" (list of rows), each row being a list of values in the same order as the header.
zebralogic.example: Wrapping the rows inside an extra "solution" key, so the verifier cannot find the required "header" and "rows" fields.

zebralogic.title: Keep Reasoning Concise to Avoid Token Truncation
zebralogic.principle: Limit explanatory text before the final JSON so that the total output stays within the model's token budget; place the solution near the end of the response.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: During the reasoning phase, before the final answer.
zebralogic.example: Writing a long paragraph of step‑by‑step deductions that pushes the JSON beyond the token limit, resulting in a truncated and invalid solution.

zebralogic.title: Preserve Original Attribute Tokens (Case and Spelling)
zebralogic.principle: Copy attribute values verbatim from the problem statement, preserving exact case, spacing, and punctuation, because the verifier matches strings exactly.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When writing the final JSON values.
zebralogic.example: Changing "google pixel 6" to "Google Pixel 6", causing a mismatch with the expected token.

zebralogic.title: Adjacency Between Name and Attribute Value
zebralogic.principle: When a clue relates a named person to an attribute of another entity (e.g., "Alice is directly left of the person whose child is Fred"), treat the attribute as representing its owner and enforce the adjacency/ordering between the named person and that owner.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a positional clue mentions a name on one side and a non‑name attribute (child, pet, car, etc.) on the other.
zebralogic.example: Placing Alice and the child Fred in the same house, ignoring that the clue requires Alice to be left of the mother of Fred.

zebralogic.description: Generating overly long reasoning before the final answer, causing the output to exceed the token limit and truncate the JSON solution.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model continues to elaborate on deductions without accounting for the fixed token budget of the response.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Keep the reasoning brief and place the JSON solution near the end, ensuring the total output stays within the model's token limit.

zebralogic.description: Providing the solution in a format not recognized by the verifier (e.g., missing "header"/"rows" keys or adding extra wrapper fields).
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model follows a generic JSON template or adds extra nesting, deviating from the exact schema expected by the verifier.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Emit exactly the two top‑level keys "header" and "rows" with the correct ordering of values, and no extra wrapper objects.

zebralogic.description: Using incorrect case or synonyms for attribute values (e.g., "German" instead of "german").
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalizes text or guesses a more natural spelling, forgetting that the verifier matches strings verbatim.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute tokens directly from the problem statement, preserving case, spacing, and punctuation.

zebralogic.description: Misinterpreting adjacency constraints that involve a named entity and a non‑name attribute (e.g., child name), treating them as non‑adjacent or placing both in the same house.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model parses the clue as a simple left‑of relation between the name and the attribute value, ignoring that the attribute belongs to another entity.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Identify the owner of the attribute, treat that owner as a separate entity, and enforce the adjacency/ordering between the named entity and the owner.
